utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the witness brought in, please. (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning to the interpreters. Does everybody hear me? Good morning, everybody. Good morning to the Defence and Prosecution counsel and to our witness. We will now resume. At the end of the morning, the registrar will tell us how many days the Prosecutor still has. We're asking Mr. Fourmy to set up the new schedule which will, among other things, take into account the arrival of the Trial Chamber's witnesses. We still have certain things that haven't been settled but things are getting clearer, and we'll try and finalise the completion of this trial at the end of July. Good morning, General Blaskic. Mr. Kehoe, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good Mr. President, Your Honours. Good morning, counsel. Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, I would like to return to our discussion about the report sent by Sliskovic to SIS at the end of September of 1993. General, in September of 1993 or the end of September 1993, who was the head of the SIS in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure who was in the SIS administration when, but I know that for a certain period of time Mr. Lucic was head of the SIS administration. Whether he was at that position in September, I'm not too sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, to whom in Mostar was Sliskovic's report sent? I'm referring to the report with the names of the perpetrators in it.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It went to the administration, the administration that was directly superior to Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Hayman, do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I think that counsel is questioning the witness about a document that is under seal, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about the report that Sliskovic sent at the end of September 1993. The report that Sliskovic sent with the names of the perpetrators. To whom was that sent?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. The question has been asked. General Blaskic, please try to focus and answer the question if you have an answer to give.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The report was sent to the administration of SIS that was directly in charge, and that is the one that was Sliskovic's direct superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is: To whom? What person? If I wasn't clear, I'm looking for a the person to whom Sliskovic sent this report.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I said that I do not know the names and the structure of the security administration. What I do know is that the report was sent to that body, the security administration that is subordinated to the Ministry of Defence, but I do not know the very personal names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. That's the answer, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, did you ask to whom Sliskovic sent this report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is precisely from Sliskovic that I asked for this report at the end of September, when he said that he sent the report to the security administration that was in charge. In this way, I thought that the security administration had taken over the case, according to what he had informed me, and that they were taking care of the case from then onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's not my question, General. My question, if it wasn't clear, I'll make it clearer. In your conversations with Sliskovic, did you ask Sliskovic the name of the person to whom he sent this report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not ask him about the name. When I asked for the report, he told me that he sent it to the security administration, the entire report and the list.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well did the Minister of Defence, Bruno Stojic, get this report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how this correspondence evolved between the security service administration that was directly subordinated to the Minister of Defence, because I was never a security official. That is a secret service that is entitled to investigate any person within the HVO, including myself and everybody else. Whether he got this or not, I do not know anything about this except for the information that I could have seen here in this courtroom from the secret document that is held under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did General Praljak, who was then chief of staff or General Petkovic, who was then the deputy chief of staff, get this report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether they got that kind of report, but I informed the chief of the main staff about that activity, that is to say, that the entire file has been handed over to the security administration that was in charge, the way the security assistant had told me, but I don't know whether he had received that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, to your knowledge, after Sliskovic sent this report with the perpetrators' names to the SIS administration in Mostar, was anyone ever punished for the crimes in Ahmici, based on that report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, according to this file, no criminal prosecution was started against the perpetrators. That is to say, this was not taken to court. I am basing this on the official knowledge I had until I came here, because I know that I could not obtain the file, nor did I hear anything about the criminal prosecution of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, was anyone disciplined, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I already talked about the practice that prevailed in the HVO. If we're talking about criminal perpetrators, then it is the law on criminal procedure that is applied, not disciplinary measures. This certainly had to do with criminal offences, and it is criminal prosecution that has to follow. In practice, disciplinary action is not taken but it is measures against criminal activity that are taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, nobody, no HVO soldier was disciplined for his conduct or involvement in the crimes in Ahmici, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I assert that the crime was a criminal offence and that that entitled criminal prosecution. I have no information as to whether any disciplinary measures were taken against someone because of the crime in Ahmici. I don't have such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Try to answer the question. The question was whether or not there were sanctions or measures taken. That's what the Prosecutor was asking.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the question, the way I heard it, was were disciplinary measures taken, that is the interpretation I got, against the perpetrator of the criminal offence in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The previous question. You answered by giving a legal interpretation on the fact that the criminal sanctions involved criminal measures as well and that moved into disciplinary measures. You've answered that. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me read you a portion of the Rules of Military Discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I am referring, Mr. President, to Article 29 of the Rules of Military Discipline. They are incorporated in Prosecutor's Exhibit 38. I believe it's tab 2, page 42. I'm just going to read, Mr. President, a brief portion of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In Article 29 -- well, before I read this, General, let me ask you a question. Do you believe it would be in the interests of the HVO to remove all HVO soldiers who were involved in any way in the crimes in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the interest of the HVO? It would have been in the interest of the HVO to remove all soldiers to committed any crime and certainly including the crime in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, let me read you the Rules of Military Discipline, Article 29 which notes as follows: "When an authorised officer establishes that a breach of military discipline is also a punishable act, the case shall be handed to an authorised prosecutor through official channels. If it is in the interest of the service, the officer shall also undertake measures to initiate disciplinary proceedings." So, General, you would agree with me that the rules under which you were bound contemplated, in the event of a crime, not only criminal Prosecution but also action to discipline the HVO soldier committing a punishable offence, isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, you read this rule to me. I'm not a lawyer, but it's clear here that it says that when an authorised officer establishes, that is to say, when he finds out what the names of the perpetrators are. Certainly if I had received the names of the perpetrators, I would have filed a criminal report against these perpetrators but the greatest problem was to get the names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That isn't the question. The question asked of you, and try to it listen carefully, you're less tired than you were yesterday, the question was whether you agree with the interpretation of that article of the rules, that is, an officer and a commander, theoretically, would be familiar with these rules. Since you yourself were in the military academy, you had notions about what this is about. We just want to know now whether you -- once the Judges have deliberated, they will take it all into account, and we're still very far from the end of the trial. Try to concentrate on the question. He's asking you a legitimate question. I'm here in order to be sure that answers are given to the questions. Either say that you don't know or say whatever you like, but at least answer the question and let's not go into theories about trains possibly meeting up with one another. There was a question about interpretation of Article 29, two paragraphs -- I've understood it correctly. I'm just discovering at the same time as you are. One of these paragraphs which provides for seizing the General Prosecutor, and the second part of that Article 29 provides, at the same time, for the possibility of issuing disciplinary measures. We're only asking whether you agree with that reading of the text. That's all that's being asked.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, I shall try to answer on the basis of the practice that existed within the HVO, that is to say, that if a soldier commits a crime, then there is a criminal report with his name and surname included, and then this is processed by the court. Possibly the soldier may be removed from the unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That's not the question that was asked. I'm sorry. You have to answer the question, otherwise, simply say that you don't want to answer it, General Blaskic. We're the not going to spend the whole day with this. We're reading an interpretation of the text for you. You could say to me, for instance, that you need to read the text. That's possible. It's a theoretical type of question for right now. You're speaking about HVO practice. We've more or less understood that that's not what was done. Mr. Kehoe, would you please go back to the text of Article 29 and -- am I speaking too quickly? We'll give the text of Article 29 to the General. Mr. Nobilo, please intervene. I really could ask for nothing better, or Mr. Hayman. Give the text to the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should be Prosecutor's Exhibit 38, tab 2. It's the Narondi Lists that we're reading, and in the tab 2, Mr. Registrar, I believe that Article 29 is on page 42 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At the same time, it will be very good for the president to have the article reread as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is in French as well, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, if it's also in French, that's even better. Thank you, Mr. Registrar. What tab is it? On tab 2, so that I can show it to my colleagues, in the French version, what text are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It is the Rules of Military Discipline, and it is page 42 in the B/C/S Narodni List.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Forty-two in B/C/S. All right. I'd like to ask for just a few seconds so that my two colleagues and I can familiarise ourselves with this. It's in French, Judge Shahabuddeen. I know that you can understand French. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that things are clear. The Judges have familiarised themselves with Article 29 which, as I have understood, has two paragraphs: one which speaks about criminal matters, and the other which is more focused on discipline. Both are connected one to the other. General Blaskic, have you had the time to read the Article, that is, Article 29? We'll ask the Prosecutor to ask you the question again. It's a theoretical question. And then you may be asked to answer practical questions, and even if the question isn't asked, your Defence counsel could say what was done in practice, which is something that you would know. Mr. Kehoe, please ask your question about Article 29.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, according to Article 29, if a soldier commits a crime, not only can he be prosecuted for that crime, but if it is in the interests of the HVO, the presiding officer or commanding officer shall initiate disciplinary proceedings as well. So there is, in fact, a dual track of criminal prosecution and disciplinary prosecutions that take place at the same time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is what it says in Article 29. Indeed, I'm not a lawyer, and I see the authorised officer, that is to say, the person who is authorised to take disciplinary measures against that soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: In the middle district of Flo -- excuse me, central district. Excuse me. Central district -- that was a throwback, Your Honour. It's a private joke that Mr. Hayman and Mr. Harmon and I have because I spent a large majority of my career as a Prosecutor in the Middle District of Florida, so my verbal faux pas that I just committed there had to do with that. What I really meant to talk about was the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. In any event, with that moment of levity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Get a hold of yourself. I know you're in a hurry to return to the United States, but nonetheless, let's become serious again and focus. The theoretical question is one that we more or less agree on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone, the person who was the presiding officer for disciplinary matters and had overall command of the military disciplinary courts was you; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was authorised for disciplinary measures against units that were directly subordinated to me, that is to say, except for the special purposes units and the military police units. I did not have any authority over them in terms of disciplinary action nor did I take any disciplinary action against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, to go back to the initial inquiry concerning the filing of this report by Sliskovic at the end of September, to your knowledge, sir, nobody was ever disciplined and nobody was ever prosecuted after the filing of that report by Sliskovic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because the problem was to get the file with the names of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us take the names of the perpetrators. Did you ask Sliskovic for the names of those perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked him to submit the entire file to me. I asked Sliskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And Sliskovic was your subordinate at the time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was not my subordinate, he was an immediate associate. He was directly subordinated to security administration because he is an officer of the security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So if Slavko Marin described Mr. Sliskovic as your subordinate, he would have been inaccurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sliskovic is my associate but directly subordinated to -- I think that this is in the evidence -- to the chief of the security administration. He is an associate of mine for security matters, but he is not directly subordinated to me but to the security administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, you told us during the course of your testimony on several occasions ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But you did appoint him to carry out the investigation.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because he was the only one who was competent to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. It's a little difficult to understand, for someone who is not from your hierarchy but the 10th of May report said that you've got to carry out the investigation. There is a superior-subordinate relationship there and it was somebody that you gave orders to. "I appoint Mr. Sliskovic as the person to carry out the investigation." We could assume there that in the chain of command in that case, he would have to report to you. Continue, please, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, after Sliskovic told you that he sent the report down to Mostar, did you go to Sliskovic or demand from Sliskovic the names of these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked him for the entire file, and he told me that he had sent the file to the administration that was in charge in Mostar and that that administration would continue the investigation; and what happened later, the officers of the security service were in this area and they were finalising the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My question is: After Sliskovic sent the report, did you go to Sliskovic and demand the names of the perpetrators, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked him for it, but I didn't ask him for the file anymore because I thought that the security administration had taken the whole thing into their own hands and that they would take care of the entire criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, after this report was sent to Mostar, did you contact anyone in SIS or contact Bruno Stojic or contact Milivoj Petkovic or General Praljak and ask these high officials to get you the names of these perpetrators? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I informed the chief of the main staff of the HVO about everything, and in the hierarchy, I was not in a position to exert pressure against those who were above me, that is to say, that my superior knew of this procedure and the security administration service was in charge of carrying out measures against anyone in the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you certainly were in a position to ask your superiors for these names, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: When this was taken over by the security administration, then it was my understanding that they would take over the investigation, and I was not in a position nor in charge to exert pressure against my superiors, even more so because this investigation could have been over my command and over myself personally, so I let the administration do their work and I thought that they would carry out the investigation and take action in terms of criminal prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, in your testimony in response to questions by my learned friend, Mr. Nobilo, you testified concerning why you insisted on the dismissal of Pasko Ljubicic. I'm referring, counsel, for record purposes, to the accused's testimony on pages 19546 and 19547. You noted that you insisted on Pasko Ljubicic's removal for, among other reasons, (1) on line 17: A One of the reasons also was certainly my fear that the crime of Ahmici could be repeated ... Another reason certainly was the fact -- And this is from line 23, I'm sorry. A Another reason certainly was the fact that I was aware that the crime in Ahmici had been planned behind my back, that I had received false reports. I had suspicions that there was a conspiracy behind it and that I had been sacrificed as the formal commander. Another reason -- now this is on 19547, your testimony at line 4, General: A Then also there was the question of crime and the struggle to combat crime in the Lasva Valley --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Judges are taking notes. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'll start that again, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: From line 4 on page 19547: A Then also there was the question of crime and the struggle to combat crime in the Lasva Valley, in which the military police was expected to have the leading and most prominent role, whereas in the military police itself, we had 100 members, according to our reports, who had criminal records. Now, General, that's what you told us was the reason -- reasons, among others, that you wanted Pasko Ljubicic removed, yet you didn't even ask your superiors to secure the names of these perpetrators so you could prevent another Ahmici, so you could find out about this conspiracy behind your back, so you could find out about these hundred criminals in the military police; you didn't do any of that, did you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, I was the only one to ask for an investigation and insist on an investigation. Also, on several occasions, I asked the assistant for security to complete the investigation, and when he informed me on the 30th of September that the file had been composed with the names of the perpetrators and everything and that he handed it over to the security service, I believed that the security service administration would bring this to an end and also criminally prosecute the perpetrators. In my chronology, I spoke of numerous insistences that the crime be investigated and that the investigation be brought to an end. In addition to that, in the Operation Pauk, I tried to make it possible to obtain that file and also I tried to make sure that the perpetrators would be prosecuted criminally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, isn't it true that while combat operations are going on in September, October, November, December 1993, you did nothing to try to find the names of these perpetrators so you could get them out of the HVO; isn't that a fact, sir?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that I was preoccupied with the combat operations, but I did everything until I received information that the file had been sent and conveyed to the security service, and it had authority over me as well. But I did ask and found out that they had gone to the spot and conducted the final throes of the investigation in 1993 and before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, knowing that there was a crime in Ahmici, do you think that the military district prosecutor would have wanted to know the names of these perpetrators so he could conduct an investigation?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That's what I thought, and I think that you can see that from the order of August when I asked him, point 1, that the case be turned over to the military district prosecutor, but I believe that the second order, which was stronger than mine, was that the case be handed over to SIS; and if we look at point 1 of the order, you will see that it was my position to turn the case over to the district military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the military district prosecutor -- let me withdraw that, I'm sorry. Given the fact that you were in a pocket, the military district prosecutor in Vitez was the only military district prosecutor who could have prosecuted these individuals; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the military district prosecutor of the military district court in Vitez, and had he received the file, he would have had to prosecute the perpetrators of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, when you didn't get these names from SIS in September, October, November, December, did you go to the military district prosecutor and say, "Mr. Prosecutor, conduct an investigation on these criminals and get them out of the HVO as soon as possible"? Did you do that, "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that sense, I did not, but I had a lot of meetings with the military district court; however, it was the practice that the military district prosecutor be sent in criminal files for identified perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, the fact of the matter is that after Sliskovic told you that the report had been sent to Mostar, you did nothing to try to get the names of the perpetrators of this crime; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not right. It is not that I didn't do anything to try to get the names, because in the operation of Pauk, the overall operations are used to try to get at the files and ensure names, and ensure prosecutions. It was the Pauk operation that was envisaged for ordinary crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that. Let's move ahead to Pauk in the chronology, now that you've brought it up, General, and talk a little bit about that. Now, Pauk was an operation that you were in charge of that started in June of 1994, and you testified to us that you expanded the mandate of Pauk to cover war crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Although I assume that the interpreters are interpreting, but I'm hearing the word "Pauk." "Pauk," of course, is not French. It's not a name that we know in French. It might be used in English or Serbo-Croat. Yes, I was asking the French interpreters to please say that it was Operation Spider. Thank you. You can speak about Operation Pauk, but I understand it better if it's Operation Spider.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, Your Honour. I just use the term "Operation Pauk" because I believe that's what the witness described it as. I think "Pauk" is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In any case, it's your language. All right. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, you were appointed and took charge of this operation in June of '94 and you, by your insistence, the mandate for Pauk was expanded to include war crimes, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time -- well, Pauk lasted from June until October of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Approximately five months; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You told us, General, that during this period of time SIS was under your command while you were investigating the crimes in Pauk?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: That the officers of SIS were sent to me and were under my command but not the administration of SIS. The administration of SIS was always under the direct command of the Ministry of Defence via the assistant Minister and sometimes directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You also told us, General, that you assigned these SIS officers to focus on crimes that occurred in Vitez, and Busovaca, and particularly in Ahmici. I'm referring to your transcript at page 19642 and 19643. Do you recall that, General? You can look, during the break, at your diary if you want to clarify that answer, but let me talk to you, General, about the SIS officer that you assigned to investigate Ahmici. Who was that SIS officer?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think his name was Mr. Sesar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is that a first name or a last name? Is that a surname name or a family name?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It's a surname, second name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, you told us that he was refused access to the Ahmici file in SIS. Who refused him access to the Ahmici file? What's the name of the person?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He informed me that his access to the file was blocked, but he did not tell me who effected this blockade and in what way, he just said that he was not able to access the file on Ahmici which existed, and he told me that he knows that the file exists but that he wasn't able to get it. He did not tell me who and in which way blocked him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, did you ask him who this person was who blocked him from getting this Ahmici report?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only did I ask him, but I also asked him to tell me in what way he was blocked and why he could not arrive at this file. His answer was that he had not succeeded in getting at the file and that he had been blocked. Did he not specifically tell me who effected this blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So Mr. Sesar refused to give you the name of the person who blocked him, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I reproduced what he told me word by word. He said, "I was blocked. I was not allowed." He asked me who set up the blockade. He did not give me any information on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, he refused to give you the name of the person who blocked him.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He did not tell me the name of the individual. You could put it that way. He did not tell me which individual had blocked him or the manner in which this blockade was implemented, but what he said was that he could not access the file because it had been blocked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, this was an act of obstruction by someone within SIS, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in any way it showed the autonomy of the security service and their independent functioning, functioning independently of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Listen to my question. The refusal to turn over this report was an act of obstruction by someone within SIS, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the blockade was an act of obstruction of my own efforts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, as the deputy chief of staff at this time, did you discuss this act of obstruction with the head of SIS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not discuss this with the head of SIS, because I was not in a position to do so, nor was it -- I had the competence to talk to the head of the SIS. He was never subordinate to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, from June 1994 until August of 1994, you were the deputy chief of staff of the HVO, and from August of 1994 through the end of Pauk in October of 1994, you were the chief of staff of the HVO, were you not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was the chief. I wasn't able to follow the dates that you mentioned but from August 1994 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that as the chief of staff of the entire HVO military, you were not in a position to discuss this act of obstruction by the chief of SIS, is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As the chief of the main staff, I was never superior to the SIS administration, at no point. So when I received this information from the security service, the offices of the security service, I realised that probably the SIS administration had other intentions probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, you told us that you were given this assignment, and after you were given this assignment and after you received this obstruction from SIS, did you take this up with President Zubak?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All the events within Operation Pauk I informed my superiors about. That is to say, I informed them about everything that happened, and I do believe that President Zubak was informed of that as well because there were war criminals that had been arrested. I can't tell you the names openly now, but there were those who were accused of war crimes, and I think they had been taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So, General, your testimony that you discussed with President Zubak this act of obstruction by SIS in their refusal to turn over the Ahmici file. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I claim that I informed President Zubak in writing about all ongoing activities. I don't know whether I spoke to him orally or not, but all my activities which were within the frameworks of the Spider operation were sent in writing to President Zubak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, what was Zubak's reaction to this act of insubordination?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know exactly because operation Pauk ended and then combat activities ensued at Kupres, and I was no longer in the same position, nor was I involved in those affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, this was the most serious crime that occurred during your military career in the Central Bosnian Operative Zone. Is it your testimony that as soon as you sent your report to Zubak about this act of insubordination, you took no further interest in the matter?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I don't say that. I don't say that it no longer interested me and, thus, the decision of December 1995, when I heard that an indictment had been raised against me, I decided to come here, but the situation and circumstances were such that I was engaged on other assignments and I was no longer in a position to have any relationships towards the SIS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, did you demand, or ask, or write in a letter, or in any way request that the people who obstructed you in SIS be disciplined in some fashion and, if you asked that, were they?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that I informed my superiors about all the activities while I was head of Operation Pauk, the more I was chief of the main staff, and then it was not my authority to do so vis-à-vis SIS. Perhaps I specified certain things but I can't recall them at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I would like to say only for us all to understand the entire issue, let me remind you, according to the personal notes I have taken, the problem was dealt with at great length at the hearing of the 25th of March. You have to understand that at that time, when you were involved in Operation Spider, you didn't have many superior above you and, if, as you confirmed and the Prosecutor said, this was the most serious crime that you experienced throughout your entire military career, one could ask several questions. In order to move things forward, I would like to say several questions were asked on the 25th of March and that personally, I don't want to ask the questions that I already did. They were asked and they're in the transcript. But I will say, in order to move things forward, that your initiative at the time of Operation Spider had been presented as positive by your Defence counsel but, at the time, we were surprised by the very few results that you obtained, despite of the fact that you had such an important position. Several months after Ahmici you had left that area and were now in a position where you could finally learn what had happened to Ahmici. We've already spoken about the organisational chart and you said that either you had no possibility of any action on SIS. I can remind you that Judge Shahabuddeen asked you to specify what your definitive position was about Ahmici, inter alia the combat position of the military police, because you had suspicions about the military police. You had so many doubts and suspicions that you were not too concerned about the investigation. At the same time, you asked that Commander Ljubicic leave. I would like to remind my colleagues that all of this was discussed in depth and in detail, so before the break, I would like the Prosecutor to ask very direct and concrete questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, to your knowledge, was anyone within SIS ever disciplined or sanctioned in any fashion for this act of insubordination?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that SIS is an institution completely apart from the main staff, and I was not in a position to know whether anybody was disciplined or sanctioned at all. I do not have any information about that because I was not in a position to have such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, at the time SIS was a part of the Ministry of Defence, was it not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not at that time. SIS was always directly within the composition of the Defence Ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, as the chief of staff of the entire HVO, is it your testimony that you have no knowledge about disciplinary proceedings that were issued or conducted against SIS members for this act of insubordination?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I personally have no knowledge about that. If we look at the schematic of organisation and structure of SIS, it was completely set apart. It was a secret service, autonomous, working according to its own rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, when you were discussing this matter with Mr. Sesar from SIS, and Mr. Sesar, as you mentioned, was the gentleman from SIS who was supposed to look into the Ahmici matter, did you insist that Mr. Sesar go up to Ahmici or any place else in Bosnia and talk to Pasko Ljubicic and interview him? Did you insist on that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I insisted that he go to the Vitez area to tour the region and to attempt to conduct an information himself, that is, to arrive at certain data. Of course, in doing so, to talk about all the perpetrators from within the military police. I did not specify all the details, but I did, of course, have in mind the commander of the military police as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, did he interview as well, Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He told me that he was not in a position to arrive at any kind of information because there was complete silence over the whole affair, and he was not able to provide me with any information. That was what he reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, Pasko Ljubicic was still in the HVO when the Pauk matter was being investigated; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't think he was in the military section of the HVO, but I'm not quite sure where he was moved to and what duties he performed. I think he was, at that time, possibly in the civilian police force. I don't think he was in the HVO, at all events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, he was in the HVO, and he was, accordingly, under the chain of command that goes back to President Zubak; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In the military part of the HVO, he was not there at that time. He was not in the military section of the HVO at that time, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, let us just go to the bottom line. To your knowledge, did Mr. Sesar interview Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sesar did not inform me that he had interviewed him, at least I don't recall him saying so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, how about Vlado Santic, the member of the military police that was down the hall from you in the Hotel Vitez; did Sesar interview him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about that. Possibly he did, possibly he did not. I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, you were in charge of this entire matter, and you don't know whether or not he interviewed Vlado Santic or not about what happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether he talked or not because I was the chief of the overall Pauk operation for the entire region of Herceg-Bosna, and we conducted many activities. There was 310 people at one point, the perpetrators of crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: How about Mario Cerkez? Did Mr. Sesar interview Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I really have no knowledge on that. Quite possibly he had an interview. Perhaps he was not satisfied with the talks, with the interview. That is possible, but I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, how about Dusko Grubesic, yet another commander, he from the Nikola Subic-Zrinjski Brigade; did Sesar interview him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Once again, I can't remember whether he did or didn't. Perhaps he talked to him. He spent some time in the area. Now, whether he specifically had talks with all those individuals, I don't know. He would just inform me briefly of the results of his talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, this particular operation was discussed in your conversations with my learned friend, Mr. Nobilo, about how you issued a particular person to go and investigate or look into Ahmici again. Did you read the interviews or the material that Sesar came back with?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sesar informed me orally about the results of his work and he submitted a report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So in this report that he submitted to you, did you read the interviews of what people said and who he interviewed?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not read the talks because he said that he had not arrived at a list of the suspects because there was a conspiracy of silence that reigned in the area. That was his report to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, after you got this report back, did you then go back to Zubak and re-emphasise the problems of this investigation and demand once and for all that the investigation be revealed and that the people be prosecuted for these outrageous crimes? Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have already stated that I informed in writing about all my activities, and this report encompassed that. When he said that he had come back from the region and reported back to me and said that he had been blocked by the officers of SIS, I sent out a report to my superiors, and I have already said that that was a crime when certain steps forward had been taken within the activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Well, General, the bottom line is that no charges were ever brought against anybody for the crimes in Ahmici and no one was ever evicted from the HVO as a result of those crimes; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is true that no charges were filed, but I profoundly believe that the investigation was conducted, the list was made up with the names of the perpetrators, and that it was kept in the SIS administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: First of all, I want to express my own appreciation for the recapitulation by President Jorda of the substance of what took place sometime in March. You were then being examined by, I think, Mr. Nobilo or Mr. Hayman and some questions were asked. Now we have been appropriately refreshed about that and we need not retrace the steps. I want to ask you some incidental questions. You referred a while ago to the fact that you voluntarily surrendered yourself to the Tribunal. Would I be right in supposing that you took the decision voluntarily to surrender on the basis that you would be able to establish your innocence? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would that mean that, at the time when you took the decision voluntarily to surrender yourself to the Tribunal, you thought that you would be in possession of all the relevant material to enable you to give proof of your innocence?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believed that my attorneys would be in a position to obtain all the documents which would enable me to prove my innocence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you take the view that the file in question which related to Ahmici would contain valuable material enabling you to put forward an effective defence and to demonstrate your innocence?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did believe in that, yes, that material and all the other documents relating to my work while I was commander of the Operative Zone in Vitez and that my attorneys would succeed in having those essential documents at least until the beginning of the trial, by the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: But whether your attorneys would succeed in gaining access to the file was a matter that was yet to come. What I want to ask you is this: Why did you decide to surrender yourself to the Tribunal without, at that point of time, being certain yourself that you would gain access to that very important file?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I profoundly believed that once the trial had got under way, my attorneys would succeed in accessing all documents that were vital to me and that there would be no blockade as regards the access of documents by my attorneys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you appreciate, at the time when you decided to surrender yourself, that your defence would be handicapped if, in fact, your counsel did not succeed in gaining access to that file?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to remember all my thoughts at that time and the dilemmas I had, whether to come to the Tribunal or not, but I clarified that dilemma as early on as November, and I think that there are witnesses to that. We did not present those witnesses, but there were witnesses with whom I discussed that dilemma. I expected that there would be difficulties, but I did not expect to have as much difficulty as possible with regard to the access of these documents, the difficulties encountered by my counsel. Perhaps I was -- perhaps I believed too much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, should the Trial Chamber understand that at the time when you took the decision to surrender to the Tribunal, you were acting on the legal advice of counsel? Did you have counsel at that point of time?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At that time, I think I did not -- I'm sure I did not have any counsel at that period of time when I made my decision, but I had good friends and I talked to them, exchanged views about everything, and regardless of everything, I decided to surrender. This was as far back as November 1995. I did not have a single attorney then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well then, General, do you accept that at the time when you decided to surrender yourself to the Tribunal, you had no basis on which to suppose that the counsel which you would later have would be able to gain access to that file?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I believed, Your Honour, that once the trial began, or perhaps during the preparation of the trial when I would come here, that the general climate would change and that there would be no problems with the attorneys getting a hold of that file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a question. Why did your chiefs put you at the head of that Operation Spider several months after the events?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know because I was not in that position. Others made that decision. They probably took into account my work, my behaviour, and everything else. This was an all-out operation against all forms of unlawfulness and against all the perpetrators of any crimes, including war crimes. They probably took into account various references and the result of my work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But when the work was given to you, one could legitimately be surprised that you, who were the operative commander at the highest level and who had experienced this tragedy at Ahmici very closely, which so moved the International Community and which you yourself denounced as a crime, one could be surprised that you did not rush immediately to the Ahmici case file.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, during the first stage, Operation Pauk was not contemplated as such that it should deal with the perpetrators of war crimes. That kind of mandate was yet to be obtained. Later, when the mandate was extended to include war crimes, I tried to obtain that file but I didn't manage to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But when was the operation extended to cover war crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After -- after -- I don't know the exact date, but perhaps in June or July or perhaps later. I cannot recall the exact date but, at any rate, after the operation had started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Summer of 1994. What number did you have in the military hierarchy? Were you in Mostar? Where were you exactly?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not in Mostar. In Posusje, that's where I was, in Posusje. That is about 60 kilometres away from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And where was SIS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were in Mostar. The SIS administration was in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: At that time, you were the deputy chief of staff of the HVO responsible for Operation Spider; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was chief of the main staff from August onward, so there was a period when I was deputy and there was a period when I was chief of the main staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So, therefore, you were number 1 in the HVO hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, but the HVO hierarchy, as far as the administration of the military police and the security service, had retained its independence, and although I held that position, I was not in charge of ordering a single military policeman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sure that that would be your answer, but that isn't really my question. My question relates somewhat to the kind of ethical and moral climate in this case. The Tribunal was established in 1993. We know that, starting in 1994, the Office of the Prosecutor began its investigations. You were shocked by what happened in Ahmici. You were in a position within the HVO which is really outstanding. Outstanding. I don't know whether we can verify this, but it's possible that SIS was not part of your hierarchy. That's possible. It doesn't really matter. It seems to me that having this problem of conscience and remorse very deeply engrained within you because, as Judge Shahabuddeen brought out and mentioned, you decided to surrender, come to The Hague, in 1995. Therefore, the problem of Ahmici was something that was haunting you, according to what you say. You were number 1 within the HVO hierarchy, and you were satisfied to have one of your collaborators say to you, "The Ahmici case file? Well, we don't know where it is." Silence. We don't talk about it. You can imagine that there is something difficult to swallow here. Do you understand what I mean when I say that? Difficult to accept, difficult to swallow. You didn't question anybody, you didn't make any telephone calls, you didn't go to see those people who were still alive after that tragedy? You didn't try to say to yourself, "Well, one day people are going to say that I'm guilty," even morally speaking, without speaking about the International Tribunal. I don't know, for your children, for your family, for posterity, for history, "History" with a capital "H." Now, you were number 1 in the hierarchy, and someone comes and says to you, "Top secret. Ahmici is top secret." And you say, "Well, all right, top secret." Is that what you're saying to us? Please answer me. Is that what you're saying? You agreed to the operation of the organisational chart as it was, "Yes" or "No"? "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not agree, and I did everything. It is clear in this file that I was the only one who insisted on an investigation and the only one who asked for an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But I'm not asking you about that moment -- we're not talking about that. We talked about yesterday, about the time when you asked for an investigation when. The Prosecutor asked you some questions about what that request for an investigation meant. The Judges are not arriving at decisions on the basis of a single piece of paper. We're trying to understand the very intimate reality of what happened, the core of what happened. I'm speaking of August 1995. Chance, perhaps not chance, put you at the head of the HVO, very close to the archives. I'm asking you to assert to me that you were satisfied with the answer from a lower-ranking individual who said to you, "General, Ahmici is not something you should touch," and you were number one in the HVO. Morally -- I'm not speaking about us, but you have your children and your family, you have posterity, the International Community which spoke about the crime at Ahmici, and you simply say "Yes." All right. All right. There is a file, because you've told us there is a file. All right. There's no more file above here. Well, the president of the republic is hiding the file. That may be, but you had assets, and that's what I don't understand. You had assets. You could make phone calls. You could write. You could have someone write for you, have Stojic write. Many people could have written for you. What I wanted to ask you, simply, was whether you could confirm to me that you accepted the fait accompli, the fact that they were not giving you the case file. You accepted people saying to you, "No, you cannot have access to the file." "Yes" or "No"? Did you accept that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I informed my superiors of what I was told, and I tried to gain access to the archives and to the file. Under those circumstances, I did whatever I could. All of those were wartime circumstances, I did whatever I could in view of my competencies and in view of my possibilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, but I have noted your answer when you said that you did everything that you could, and that's the kind of answer that I would like. All right. It's marked in the -- it's put in the transcript. You did what you could do. I think that Judge Rodrigues had some questions before the break, I think. Then we'll finish with that point. Very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General Blaskic, I would like to go back to April 1993 and the following months and ask you, from the military point of view, what were the consequences in respect of the combat which was going on in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the consequences were, at any rate, a great number of victims on both sides, great destruction, and a situation without a way out that we were facing then. Just about to be totally destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. I'm speaking about the consequences, the subsequent repercussions and consequences on the development of what happened, that is, the future evolution and development of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I'll ask the question a different way. Imagine that there never been an Ahmici. Could something else have happened, in military terms?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Would you please clarify this a bit to me, this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps I could ask the question -- maybe I'll ask the question after the break. Maybe that would be better. You could rest a little bit. I think, Mr. President, this is the time to allow the witness to rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I think everybody needs a bit of a rest. We'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. We'll resume the hearing now. Judge Rodrigues, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, were you able to rest a little bit?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: This is my question -- I don't want to lead the answer but perhaps I could ask my question in the following way: Perhaps Ahmici was something which really made the Muslims angry and, therefore, the way that the battles took place and the fighting took place after that must be seen in the light of what happened in Ahmici. As a military man, what is your opinion about that? Could we say that there were repercussions on the development of the combat in Central Bosnia because of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, certainly there were. That can certainly be seen by the number of casualties, so many casualties in such a small space. Of course, this did cause a strong reaction on the part of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as I was thinking during this break, I remembered that from the first incidents onwards, the first spiral of violence went up. I talked about the conflict at Duhri here, and now that I think of it, violence was always on the rise. This probably made a cease-fire with the army more difficult or, at least, there was a slow-down. I do not know all the political arrangements that were made between the representatives of the three peoples, but I believe that during a certain period of time there was a concept that prevailed and that we saw from a piece of evidence that the Prosecutor showed to me, and that was that the Croats were supposed to disappear from that area, that is to say, from the area of Central Bosnia. However, at any rate, this only led to the increase of the dimensions and scope of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Here's the other question. You told us that you were very concerned about the fighting, about the refugees and so on, and that you didn't have time to pay much attention to Ahmici. So here's my question: Was there any time when you thought that you should say to your superiors something like that or like this rather; "Somebody carried out my assignment -- someone like myself has difficulty carrying out his responsibilities. I'm not responsible for Ahmici. Either you explain to the opposing party what happened and punish the perpetrators in such a way as to calm down our enemies or I'm going to leave." Did you ever think that or say that to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I sent many reports to my superiors about the problems in that spirit. Perhaps not word-for-word everything you just said, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Pardon me. My question is trying to ascertain whether you, as a way of putting pressure, as a way of putting pressure, whether you set forth the possibility of your resigning before your superiors if they did not explain what happened in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In those moments I was not in that kind of a situation, and I already said that in these moments of combat I did not contemplate resignation, that is to say, when we were encircled, but I did tell my superior that he had to change and break down the chain of command in the military police, because it was my suspicion that the members of the military police committed the crime in Ahmici. I just wish to add one more thing, Your Honour. It is not that I thought that I didn't have enough time to deal with Ahmici and the investigation. I said that at that time I had other problems and priorities as well, that is to say, other jobs to do. I also said that I was not a professional in that sense and that I was not trained to carry out an investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, but all of those concerns, and all the fighting, and all the refugees were the result of Ahmici. Therefore, had you resolved the issue of Ahmici, perhaps you would have resolved all the other problems.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I wish I did have the command, authority, and power to resolve Ahmici, and I wish Ahmici had never happened. However, I already said that this spiral was an ongoing thing. Ahmici is a major crime but, regrettably, not the first crime that was committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Could the conclusion then be that yesterday you said that you were very proud of having remained, very proud of not having resigned, but does that mean that you also assumed the responsibility of remaining?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know which responsibility you have in mind, because in the military there are several responsibilities, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Well, I'm thinking about the moral responsibility that the Presiding Judge spoke about.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I was aware of the situation that I was in in that encirclement and, indeed, this was a situation where no way out was in sight. I don't want to tire the Honourable Court, but perhaps it would be easiest to describe this in one line only. Everything that was abnormal was going on in that area. It was a wonder, a miracle when we heard of a man dying of a natural death, not having been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But didn't you realise that you were surrounded in every sense? You were militarily surrounded. You were surrounded by people who apparently shared the same objectives, that is, the military police. The Ministry of Defence had also surrounded you, had also encircled you. Didn't you realise that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if I'm going to be able to answer your question. I was totally encircled and before total destruction, in a military sense, in that area, that is to say, that destruction was imminent. I'm trying to say that I was struggling for survival day after day. Also, when the Washington Agreement came about, I think that it was most comprehensively realised and in the quickest possible way in that area, in the Lasva River Valley.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Rodrigues. We are at the heart of many issues now. Excuse us, Mr. Prosecutor, for having interrupted you. I know that many of these questions were asked during the examination-in-chief, and that will help us at the end of the cross-examination and the redirect. Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. Were you able to find the thread of what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: General, we're going to continue on with your efforts in Operation Pauk, and I'd like you to take a look at a Defence exhibit at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, Defence 255. Yes. That's it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, during the course of your direct-examination, you discussed this particular article with my colleague, Mr. Nobilo, and noted for us that Ivica Rajic and others were arrested during your Operation Pauk.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, Rajic was not arrested for war crimes, was he? He was arrested for the murder of some HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was arrested with all the materials that were there, and everything was handed over to the military prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a newspaper article from the 8th of September, 1995, and this newspaper article, General, comes from Nedjeljna Dalmacija, as I noted, from the 8th of September, 1995. Mr. President, Your Honours, this periodical, Nedjeljna Dalmacija, I understand is a Croatian weekly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecutor's Exhibit 698, 698A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Take a look at this document, General. This particular article, as you peruse through it, General, reflects that Ivica Rajic and Dominik Ilijasevic (Como), as well as Vlatko Trogrlic (Zuna), were arrested for the murder of HVO soldiers, Zeljko Bosnjak; Ivica, sometimes referred to as Marko, Pecirep, and also the murders of Davor Lovric and Zvonko Duznovic. Now, all of these victims, General, were Croats; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. This is about how the district military prosecutor took action against these persons who were arrested on the basis of all the materials that were available at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, in the exhibit that we talked about before, Defence 255 -- Mr. Usher, if we could just give that particular article back to the witness, that is the Defence Exhibit which is the article from Slobodna Dalmacija -- in that article, Ivica Rajic admits being involved in Stupni Do, does he not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have two pages. Could you please tell me on which page this is?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first page. The first page, sir. As the interview with Rajic transpires, it is the fourth question. The note says: "On the night before the HVO operation in Stupni Do Muslim special forces allegedly arrived in the village, and were preparing a final attack on Vares. "Yes, that is correct." And then Rajic discusses Stupni Do. Do you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I have found it, yes, yes. I'm reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, Stupni Do was a horrific, horrific war crime, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Stupni Do was a war crime about which I received information indirectly and only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me show you a series of photographs. And, Mr. President, I might ask, Mr. President, to caution the individuals in the crowd that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We'll go back to that. I would like to understand something. The question that you are preparing has to do with a comparison with the two press articles?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The first article, the article that was submitted by the Defence, Exhibit 255, notes that Ivica Rajic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And what he had been charged with, Mr. President, was he was charged with the murders of Bosnian Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Stupni Do, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Stupni Do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Ivica Rajic was never charged by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The murder of HVO officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Correct. And what I have, Mr. President, is a series of photographs taken by the British battalion, or a non-commissioned officer in the British battalion, just a series of photographs on Stupni Do taken the 23rd of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The massacre of Stupni Do taken by the British battalion. You're going to show them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I just ask, Mr. President, that we might caution the audience because some of these photographs are quite explicit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The public has been informed. These are photographs that are going to be shown. These are public hearings, but as the Prosecutor says, these are very difficult pictures to look at. Those people who are particularly sensitive might want to leave the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: A question for Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Will this be one document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: With slashes, the same exhibit with slashes; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. That's probably easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. All right. Let's go on. All right. Perhaps you could prepare the material. This is taking a bit of time and we're really using up too much time here. This should have been prepared this morning. Let me point this out to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is my fault, Mr. President. I apologise. I should have done it ahead of time and I didn't and I take full blame for it. It's not the registrar's fault. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have no disciplinary powers over you, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Judge. I should have done it, and I know I should have. I apologise for the delay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Very well. All right. Mr. Registrar, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 699, 699/1, 699/2, 699/3, 699/4, and 699/5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, if we could put these in seriatim on the ELMO, Mr. President? As I noted, these are the photographs taken by a non-commissioned officer of the British battalion on the 23rd. The first photograph, Mr. Usher, is an overall view of the village of Stupni Do. If we can go to the next one? 699/2 is just another angle of the village. 699/3 is similar, just a different angle of the village. Can we go to the next one, Mr. Usher? Yet another angle. The next one. This is an examination, a photograph of some of the bodies. Continue on, Mr. Usher. Next photograph. That, I believe, is 699/4. That's another body photograph. Continue on, please. These are two -- three women huddled in a house that we will talk about in a subsequent report, Mr. President. The next one, Mr. Usher, please. This is an old man, of course, shot. And the last -- is that the last one? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, General, let us, before we talk about these individual photographs, let us turn to some reports from the ECMM first. Mr. President, this is an ECMM report dated the 27th of October, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is Prosecution Exhibit 700.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, I'm interested in the bottom of the page under "Other Matters," number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, dealing with "Other Matters," number 6 deals with the massacre at Stupni Do. It notes that: "This report should be read in conjunction with CC Travnik DR 26 Oct 93. "V4 joined an UNPROFOR convoy which went to Stupni Do together with two television crews. The UNPROFOR led force was denied access by the HVO, and responded by forcing entry, with NORDBAT -- That's Nordic Bat. "-- troops moving mines and crushing roadblocks. The village is destroyed, and no survivors remain. Twenty bodies had been found by the end of the day, the search will continue tomorrow. "Most of the bodies found so far were burned beyond recognition, however three were identified as men, and three as middle aged women; some shot in the head, and some with their throats cut. It is presumed that some of the burned bodies were children by the size of the skull parts. Signs of torture, by burning, were observed on some of the bodies." Could we turn the page, Mr. Usher, please? Top of the page: "The Chief of Staff of UNPROFOR BH Command stated to the media that the evidence indicated war crimes; which would be further investigated, and reported to the War Crimes Commission in Geneva." We can skip a paragraph and start with "Witnesses": "Witnesses claim that the HVO began arresting all males in Vares over the age of 16 on 23 Oct., and that beatings and rapes were inflicted on others. Muslims in Vares believe that the atrocities were committed by HVO from Kiseljak ... but that they had to have had the assistance of local HVO authorities, given the well organised round of Muslim males. "Based on reports that Muslims are being held and abused in the Vares elementary school V4 attempted, but was denied, access by the HVO. A NORDBAT platoon commander who attempted to support ECMM's access reported a strong smell of disinfectant in the entrance of the school. "V4 will return tomorrow to determine the fate and status of Muslims remaining in Vares." "Assessment." "Evidence to date indicates that the action in Stupni Do was not a spontaneous event, but rather carefully planned and orchestrated. The motive remains unclear. The HVO LO --" That's "liaison officer." "-- in Vitez told HCC that they had little information from the Vares area, but that contrary to other reports, the commander HVO Bobovac Brigade had been replaced; and his successor has yet to be named. "Graphic details of the massacre appeared on local television tonight, and the full gamut of response, from reaction to retaliation, must be expected. BiH commanders may have difficulty controlling not only radical factions, but also regular troops. "Croat leaders who have been complaining that world media have been ignoring them will have difficulty dealing with this new image." If I can turn to another exhibit, Mr. President, and this is an excerpt from the 17 November 1993 report of Ambassador Mazowiecki on Commission of Human Rights, and this has one pertinent paragraph concerning Stupni Do. If I might give that to the usher for distribution. Mr. President, this was published in French as well as English. I will obtain the French copy as well. I just, with some time constraints, was unable to get it from the human rights --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Mazowiecki report?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.
